questions.q: Pointing to a woman in a photograph, Rohan said, “Her husband's mother is the only daughter-in-law of my father's father's father.” Rohan's father has exactly one brother, who is unmarried. How is the woman related to Rohan?
questions.solution: Father's father's father = Rohan's great-grandfather. His only daughter-in-law is the wife of his married son, Rohan's grandfather: Rohan's grandmother. The woman's husband is a son of Rohan's grandmother, so either Rohan's father or his uncle. The uncle is unmarried, so the husband is Rohan's father and the woman is Rohan's mother.

questions.q: A test has 60 questions. Each correct answer earns 1 mark, each wrong answer costs 1/3 mark, and each unattempted question costs 1/6 mark. A student's net score is 37. At least how many questions did the student answer wrongly?
questions.solution: Multiply by 6: 6c − 2w − u = 222 with c + w + u = 60, so 7c − w = 282, i.e. w = 7c − 282. Need w ≥ 0, so c ≥ 41 (c = 41 gives w = 5, u = 14). Check c = 40: w = −2, impossible. Minimum w = 5.

questions.q: A clock is set right at 9:00 a.m. on Monday. It loses 12 minutes every 24 hours, at a uniform rate. What is the correct time when this clock shows 5:00 p.m. on Wednesday?
questions.solution: The clock shows 1428 minutes for every 1440 real minutes. Shown time elapsed = 56 h, so real time = 56 × 1440/1428 = 56.47 h ≈ 56 h 28 min 14 s after Monday 9:00, i.e. Wednesday 5:28:14 p.m. Trap: subtracting 12 min/day × 2⅓ days instead of using the rate.

The LCM of a positive integer N and 756 is 7,560, and the HCF of N and 600 is 120. What is the sum of the digits of the smallest possible N?
questions.solution: 756 = 2²·3³·7 and 7560 = 2³·3³·5·7, so N must contain 2³ and 5 (756 lacks them), with 3 ≤ 3³ and 7 ≤ 7¹. 600 = 2³·3·5², and HCF = 120 = 2³·3·5, so N has exactly 5¹ and at least one 3. Smallest: 2³·3·5 = 120. Check: LCM(120, 756) = 7560 ✓. So N = 120, digit sum 3.

questions.q: How many odd integers n with 300 ≤ n ≤ 700 are divisible by neither 3 nor 11?
questions.solution: Odd numbers 301…699: 200. Odd multiples of 3: 303…699 → 67. Odd multiples of 11: 319…693 → 18. Odd multiples of 33: 363…693 → 6. Answer = 200 − 67 − 18 + 6 = 121.

questions.q: Six interns I1–I6 are to be assigned to six projects P1–P6, one intern per project. P1 cannot go to I1 or I2; P2 must go to I3 or I4; and I5 cannot work on P3. In how many ways can the assignment be made?
questions.solution: P2: 2 choices (I3 or I4). P1: one of I3–I6 other than P2's intern, so 3 choices. Case 1: P1 = I5 (1 way). The other 4 interns fill P3–P6 freely: 24. Case 2: P1 is one of the other 2. I5 is among the remaining 4 and must avoid P3: 24 − 6 = 18 each, so 36. Total = 2 × (24 + 36) = 120. Trap: 2 × 3 × 24 = 144 ignores the I5 restriction.

questions.q: 1,240 balls form a complete square pyramid (1 ball on top, 4 in the next layer, 9 in the next, and so on). The same balls are re-stacked as a triangular pyramid (1, 3, 6, 10, … per layer) with as many complete layers as possible. How many balls are left over?
questions.solution: Square pyramid: n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = 1240 gives n = 15. Triangular pyramid: k(k+1)(k+2)/6 ≤ 1240. k = 18 gives 1140; k = 19 gives 1330, too many. Left over = 1240 − 1140 = 100.

questions.q: Pipes P, Q and R together fill an empty tank. P is open throughout. Q is open only for the first 12 minutes. R is opened 3 minutes after Q is closed and stays open until the tank is full. Each pipe fills exactly one-third of the tank. If P and Q had both been kept open throughout, the tank would have filled in the same total time. How long would R alone take to fill the tank?
questions.solution: Q fills 1/3 in 12 min, so Q = 1/36 per min. Let the total time be T. P fills 1/3 in T, and (P + Q) × T = 1 gives 1/3 + T/36 = 1, so T = 24. R runs from minute 15 to minute 24 (9 min) and fills 1/3, so R alone takes 27 min.

questions.q: A boat 45 km from the harbour springs a leak that lets in 2 tonnes of water every 8 minutes. The boat will sink once 84 tonnes of water are inside. Its pump removes 8 tonnes per hour. What is the minimum average speed at which the boat must travel to reach the harbour just before it would sink?
questions.solution: Leak = 2 t per 8 min = 15 t/h. Net inflow = 15 − 8 = 7 t/h. Time to 84 t = 12 h. Speed = 45/12 = 3.75 km/h. Trap: ignoring the pump gives 84/15 = 5.6 h → 8.04 km/h.

questions.q: Riya buys some mangoes and finds 3 of them rotten, which she throws away. She keeps four-sevenths of the rest and gives the remaining mangoes to her neighbour, who eats 2 and stores the rest in a basket that cannot hold more than 7 mangoes. What is the maximum number of mangoes Riya could have bought?
questions.solution: Good mangoes G must be a multiple of 7. The neighbour gets 3G/7, eats 2, so 3G/7 − 2 ≤ 7 → G ≤ 21. Max G = 21, bought = 21 + 3 = 24.

questions.q: Seven positive integers have a mean of 15 and a median of 14, and their only mode is 10. What is the largest possible value of the greatest of these integers?
questions.solution: Sum = 105, middle value 14. To maximise the largest, make the others as small as possible. Two 10s are needed for the mode (1, 10, 10), so no other value may appear twice: the values above the median must be 15 and 16, not 14 again. 1 + 10 + 10 + 14 + 15 + 16 = 66, so the largest = 105 − 66 = 39. (Using three 10s with 14 repeated gives only 32.)

questions.q: Positive integers x, y and z satisfy xy = 360 and yz = 150, with z < 10. What is the minimum possible value of x + y + z?
questions.solution: y divides both 360 and 150, so y divides 30, and x/z = 360/150 = 12/5. Try y = 30 → x = 12, z = 5: sum 47. y = 15 → x = 24, z = 10, but z < 10 fails. Smaller y makes x much larger. Minimum = 47.

What is the average of all the distinct 4-digit numbers that can be formed using the digits 3, 3, 5 and 0, each exactly once?
questions.solution: Distinct arrangements = 4!/2! = 12, minus those starting with 0 (3!/2! = 3), so 9 numbers. Their sum is 35,442, so the average is 3,938.00. Shortcut: count how often each digit sits in each place.

questions.q: The author would most likely agree that a road widening after which average travel time returns to its earlier level:
options: was a waste of public money
may still have succeeded if the corridor now carries more trips
proves that induced demand makes all road projects futile
should be followed by further widening to finally beat congestion
shows that travellers misjudge the time cost of driving
questions.solution: Para 3: a widening 'can raise the total number of trips a corridor carries, which may be precisely the point'; judging by speed alone is 'the error'. A and C are the extreme readings the author explicitly rejects ('None of this means that roads are useless'). D is the mistake the author criticises.
questions.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, traffic engineers treated congestion as a plumbing problem: if too many cars were trying to squeeze through a pipe, the obvious remedy was a wider pipe. The logic seemed unassailable, and cities from Los Angeles to Bengaluru poured concrete accordingly. Yet the data stubbornly refused to cooperate. Within a few years of a road being widened, travel times on it frequently returned to where they had been, and sometimes grew worse.

Economists call this phenomenon induced demand. A road, like any other good, is consumed more when its price falls, and the price of a road is paid chiefly in time. When a new lane cuts a commute from fifty minutes to thirty, people who had previously avoided the trip, by travelling off-peak, taking the train, or simply not going, begin to drive. Others move further out, confident that the faster road will absorb the extra distance. The new capacity is not wasted; it is filled, and the filling restores the very delay that justified it.

None of this means that roads are useless or that every expansion fails. A widening that relieves a genuine bottleneck can raise the total number of trips a corridor carries, which may be precisely the point. The error lies in judging success by speed alone. A city that adds lanes and measures nothing but travel time will conclude that it has failed, then add more lanes, mistaking a symptom of success, more people moving, for a disease.

The more useful question, critics argue, is not how to make driving faster but how to make the city's scarce space carry the most people. Measured that way, a single bus lane or metro line often outperforms a highway widening that costs ten times as much.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the persistence of failing projects is:
options: partly a rational response to how blame is assigned within organisations
caused by textbook economics being wrong
more common in software than in other industries
evidence that past spending reliably predicts future success
questions.solution: 'Part of this is psychological... But part is institutional': finishing protects the manager from blame, which is rational for her. A says 'entirely' (passage says 'part'). E twists 'predicts whether a project continues' into 'predicts success'.
questions.passage: A manager who has already spent Rs 40 lakh on a failing software project faces a choice: spend Rs 10 lakh more to finish it, or abandon it. Textbook economics says the Rs 40 lakh is irrelevant: it is gone whichever way she decides, so only future costs and benefits should count. Yet studies of real organisations find that the size of past spending is one of the best predictors of whether a project continues. Part of this is psychological: abandoning a project feels like admitting an error. But part is institutional. A manager who quietly cancels a project absorbs the blame for the whole Rs 50 lakh decision, while one who finishes it and fails can at least claim to have seen it through.

questions.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the institutional explanation offered in the passage?
options: Many software projects run over budget.
Finishing a project sometimes leads to its success.
Failing projects are continued just as often when the decision is taken anonymously by a committee, so no individual can be blamed.
questions.solution: The institutional explanation says persistence happens because of blame. If persistence is unchanged when nobody can be blamed, blame is not driving it, which weakens that explanation. The other options are irrelevant to the blame mechanism.
questions.passage: A manager who has already spent Rs 40 lakh on a failing software project faces a choice: spend Rs 10 lakh more to finish it, or abandon it. Textbook economics says the Rs 40 lakh is irrelevant: it is gone whichever way she decides, so only future costs and benefits should count. Yet studies of real organisations find that the size of past spending is one of the best predictors of whether a project continues. Part of this is psychological: abandoning a project feels like admitting an error. But part is institutional. A manager who quietly cancels a project absorbs the blame for the whole Rs 50 lakh decision, while one who finishes it and fails can at least claim to have seen it through.

questions.q:
Arrange the sentences into a coherent paragraph.

A. The result was a fleet that looked impressively large on paper but spent much of its time waiting for spare parts.
B. In the 1990s, several state transport undertakings bought buses from whichever supplier quoted the lowest price.
C. Maintenance crews, faced with a dozen incompatible models, could not stock parts for all of them.
D. Each tender was judged on its own, with no thought given to what the depot already owned.
E. Later procurement policies therefore began to weigh the cost of ownership, not just the purchase price.
questions.solution: B opens (sets time and context). D explains how buying happened (tender by tender), which creates the 'dozen incompatible models' in C. A is the result, E the policy response ('therefore'). Trap BCDAE: C's 'dozen models' needs D first.

questions.q:
Arrange the sentences into a coherent paragraph.

A. Yet their low cost comes with a catch: they are rarely worth repairing.
B. Small satellites in very low orbits have become the darlings of the space industry.
C. Because they sit so close to Earth, they need less powerful transmitters and cheaper launches.
D. A satellite that fails is simply written off, and its replacement must wait for the next rideshare launch.
E. For operators, this means building in redundancy from the start rather than relying on repair.
questions.solution: B introduces; C gives the reason they're cheap; A turns ('Yet... low cost') to the catch; D illustrates 'not worth repairing'; E is the consequence. 'Yet' in A needs the advantage (C) before it.

questions.q:
Find the part with an error.

Neither the manager nor his assistants (A) / was aware that the audit (B) / had been scheduled for (C) / the first week of March. (D)
questions.solution: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'assistants' (plural), so 'were aware', not 'was'. Error in B.

questions.q:
Find the part with an error.

The committee has submitted its report, (A) / which, along with the minutes of the meetings, (B) / are expected to be tabled (C) / in the next session. (D)
questions.solution: 'which' refers to 'report' (singular). 'Along with the minutes' is a parenthetical phrase and does not change the number, so it should be 'is expected'. The plural 'minutes' right before the verb is the trap.

questions.q: The new policy is aimed ____ reducing paperwork, but critics say it will result ____ more delays.
questions.solution: Fixed prepositions: 'aimed at' + -ing, 'result in' (cause). 'Result into' is a common Indian-English error, which is why 'at, into' is the trap.

questions.q: The proposal was technically sound; ____, it was rejected, ____ the board felt the timing was wrong.
questions.solution: Blank 1 needs contrast (sound, yet rejected): nevertheless/however. Blank 2 needs a reason: because. 'however, unless' fails on blank 2, and 'therefore' and 'consequently' fail on blank 1.

questions.q: The branch of linguistics that studies the formation and internal structure of words:
questions.solution: Morphology = structure/formation of words. Etymology = origin and history of words (the closest trap); Phonology = sound systems; Semantics = meaning; Philology = historical study of language in texts.

questions.q: Government by the least qualified or most unprincipled citizens:
questions.solution: Kakistocracy (Greek kakistos = worst). Ochlocracy = mob rule (the near trap); Kleptocracy = rule by thieves; Plutocracy = the wealthy; Gerontocracy = the old.

questions.q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: con-sci-en-tious-ness: 'sci' as in science, '-tious' as in cautious, double 's' at the end.

questions.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to PUSILLANIMOUS.
questions.solution: Pusillanimous = lacking courage (Latin pusillus 'very small' + animus 'spirit'). 'Petty' tempts because of 'pusill-' = small; 'indecisive' is near but not the meaning.
